docs.title: SASjs Server
docs.text:
Your SAS installation, on the web.

Run SAS programs from a browser, call them over HTTP, and give analysts somewhere to try things out - on desktop SAS, on SAS 9, or on Viya.

SASjs Server is a small NodeJS service that sits beside your SAS executable and does one job: it takes a request, runs the program, and hands back the log and the result.

Install SASjs Server Explore the API

Node 22 or later. MIT licence. Windows, macOS and Linux.

docs.title: SASjs Studio
docs.text:
A code editor in the browser that runs against your real SAS installation. The log and the webout come back in the same window, and files save to the drive.

About Studio

docs.title: REST API
docs.text:
Every action is an HTTP call: run a stored program, read a folder, upload a file. The reference doubles as a console, so you can try a call before writing any code.

Browse the API

docs.title: App Stream
docs.text:
Publish a SAS-backed web app to anyone who can sign in. Compile it with the SASjs CLI, upload the zip, and share the URL.

About App Stream

docs.title: Stored Programs
docs.text:
Keep SAS, JS, Python and R programs on the drive and run them by name, the way a Stored Process Server does.

Stored Programs

docs.title: What happens to a request
docs.text:
1. Something calls the API - this interface, a SASjs app, a script, a scheduled job. Every call is an ordinary HTTP request to a path such as /SASjsApi/stp/execute.
  2. The server runs the program in a SAS session, choosing the runtime from the program's file extension.
  3. The log and the returned data - the webout - come back in the response.

The API is the one @sasjs/adapter already speaks, so a SASjs app points at SASjs Server without a code change. A stored program typically answers in around 200 milliseconds.

docs.title: When it is the right tool
Reach for it when
docs.text:
• You have Base SAS, desktop SAS, or SAS 9 without a Stored Process Server.
  • You want SAS behind a web app, a CI pipeline, or a chat bot.
  • You want one place where analysts can run code, keep it, and share the result.
  • You need to run tests against your SAS jobs, services and macros.
  • You want to install a third-party app such as Data Controller for SAS.

docs.title: You probably do not need it if
docs.text: You run Viya's Job Execution Service or a SAS Stored Process Server. Those do this job, and SASjs Server overlaps with them rather than replacing them.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
npx @sasjs/server

The server reads .env from the directory it runs in. Two settings start it: SAS_PATH, the full path to sas.exe or sas.sh, and HTTP_PORT for the listener. Installation covers the standalone executable, keeping the process running, and the first sign-in.

docs.title: Where everything lives
docs.text:
Everything the interface links to is at a top-level path:

Path What it is / The interface: the dashboard, the Apps screen, Studio /studio SASjs Studio, running ad hoc code /apps The apps the signed-in caller may open /docs This documentation, inside the interface (the pages themselves are at /documentation) /api The REST API's reference, inside the interface (the Swagger page is at /api-assets/); the API answers /api/info, /api/stp/execute, ... /app/<name> A published App Stream application

SASjs Server is MIT open source. The repository is sasjs/server on GitHub.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
SASjs Server speaks REST under /SASjsApi, and the specification below is the same one a running server publishes at /swagger.yaml (and renders at /SASjsApi/). Every release ships its own copy, so the reference always describes the endpoints that release actually has.

The specification is checked in as docs/pages/swagger.yaml and rendered here at build time. docs/scripts/check-server-docs.mjs fails the build when that copy has drifted from the release these pages document, so the reference cannot quietly fall behind the code.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
In MODE=server every endpoint except /SASjsApi/info and /SASjsApi/auth/* needs a credential:

Caller Credential a script or server Authorization: Bearer <access_token>, from POST /SASjsApi/auth/token a browser app the session cookie the login page sets

MODE=desktop is single-user and unauthenticated, so calls need no header at all. See Authentication for the token, refresh and OIDC details, and Authorisation for the per-user and per-group rules that decide who may call what.

docs.title: Try it out
docs.text:
The reference is a static render of the specification: this site has no server behind it, so "Try it out" cannot reach an instance from here. To send the calls, open /SASjsApi/ on a running server - it serves the same specification with a live Swagger UI, and the request goes to that instance.

The examples in Deployment show the equivalent curl calls.

docs.title: App Stream
docs.text: AppStream is the gateway to apps on SASjs Server.

docs.title: Creating Apps
docs.text: Anybody can create an app for SASjs Server - it just needs to be compiled using the SASjs CLI. The output of this process is a zip file that can be imported to any SASjs Server instance.

docs.title: Deploying Apps
docs.text:
Simply click the "Upload New App" button and select the local zip file containing the app you wish to deploy.

Alternative deployment approaches include:

  • sasjs deploy - https://cli.sasjs.io/deploy/
  • Use the /SASjsApi/drive/deploy/upload API
  • Use the /SASjsApi/drive/deploy API

docs.title: Deployment limits
docs.text:
A deploy is measured before anything is written, and refused with 413 when the tree is over any of these:

Limit Value Entries 10,000, folders included Total size 100 MB, decoded A single file 20 MB

The refusal names the limit and the figure it reached, for example The file tree exceeds the deploy limit: 10001 entries (maximum 10000). Nothing is written before the checks pass, so a refused deploy leaves the drive exactly as it was.

Sizes are decoded bytes. A file member travels as its own text, or as base64 when it says encoding: "base64" - four characters for every three bytes - so a tree at the total limit with binary members is up to a third larger on the wire than on the drive, and the transport admits that much. POST /SASjsApi/drive/deploy/upload applies the same limits to the tree it unpacks from the archive, not to the archive itself.

Member names are checked in the same pass: a name carrying /, \ or .. would write outside the deployment folder, so the tree is refused with 400 instead.

docs.title: Publishing a folder of files
docs.text:
An app does not need a compiled service pack. POST /SASjsApi/drive/deploy/upload takes a zip whose entries are the files to serve:

# the archive holds the app's files, rooted where the server serves them from:
#   services/web/index.html, services/web/app.js, assets/logo.png
curl -X POST "https://my-server/SASjsApi/drive/deploy/upload?appLoc=/Public/apps/harness&streamWebFolder=web" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -F "file=@harness.zip"

The archive's structure is kept under appLoc. What a deploy document would have said comes from the query: appLoc is required, streamWebFolder publishes that folder as an App Stream app, and streamServiceName sets its label.

An app is served from <appLoc>/services/<streamWebFolder>, so that is where its entry page lives - the example above holds services/web/index.html. The same rule holds for POST /SASjsApi/drive/deploy with a JSON tree: a request that names streamWebFolder must carry that folder, and is refused with a message naming it rather than deployed, because publishing it would advertise an app that resolves to nothing.

A zip that contains a deploy document - a root-level JSON file naming appLoc or fileTree - is read as a document instead, so the route answers both shapes. A file naming only one of the two is refused with the missing field named. A JSON file the app itself ships, such as a manifest or a data file, names neither and is deployed with the rest.

Two kinds of entry are dropped, because macOS adds them to an archive of a folder and they are not part of the app: anything under __MACOSX/, and .DS_Store.

docs.title: The app's id, and the label it is known by
docs.text:
A publish gives an app its identity. The first publish of a deployment mints a UUID, and that id is the app: its URL is /app/<id>/, a removal names it, and a redeploy of the same folder keeps it - so a new bundle never moves an app's URL. The deploy answer states it as app: { id, name, url }.

The name is a label and only a label. It is what the tile says, and it may be shared: two folders may both be called report, because nothing addresses an app by its name. When streamServiceName is absent the label is the last segment of appLoc as it is spelled - /Public/apps/dashdemo publishes as dashdemo.

docs.title: The bundle's manifest
docs.text:
A compiled app may describe itself, in sasjs.app.json at the root of the archive:

{
  "name": "Dashboard",
  "streamWebFolder": "web",
  "logo": "assets/logo.png",
  "frameAncestors": ["https://example.com"]
}

streamWebFolder is the folder under <appLoc>/services holding the app's web assets; name, logo and frameAncestors are optional. The manifest describes the app rather than serving it, so it is read and left out of the deployment, and the request wins where both speak - a caller naming a folder or a label is correcting the archive. The SASjs CLI writes the manifest into the deploy tree when a target has a stream configuration.

docs.title: Removing an app
docs.text: DELETE /SASjsApi/drive/deploy takes { "id": "<id>" } and nothing else. The app stops being advertised and stops being served; the deployment's files stay in the drive, because deleting those is DELETE /SASjsApi/drive/folder.

docs.title: Replacing the folder
docs.text:
POST /SASjsApi/drive/deploy takes replace: true to write the tree as the folder's whole contents: the folder is removed before the tree is written, so a file the new version renamed or dropped stops being served. An archive upload replaces by default - publishing a folder means the folder is what the archive says it is - and ?replace=false keeps what is already there.

The removal happens after the tree is accepted, so a request that is going to be refused never deletes anything. A folder can hold more than one published app, and replacing it empties the folder, not just the app being deployed.

docs.title: Text and binary file members
docs.text:
A file member carries the caller's own text by default. An asset that is not text states encoding: "base64", and its code is base64 of the bytes to write:

{
  "members": [
    { "name": "index.html", "type": "file", "code": "<h1>Hello</h1>" },
    { "name": "logo.png", "type": "file", "encoding": "base64", "code": "iVBORw0..." }
  ]
}

Nothing is guessed from the contents: test and data are both valid base64, so a guess would corrupt short text rather than decode a file. An archive upload marks every entry base64, because an archive holds bytes.

A deploy document written by a client older than @sasjs/api 0.24 states no encoding and carries its files as base64, which this server now reads as text - so such a document has to add encoding: "base64" to each file member. The CLI states it for the assets it builds.

docs.title: The app's URL
docs.text:
An app answers on two URLs.

  • /AppStream/<id> - the id is a UUID, minted when the folder is first published and kept when it is published again, so this URL survives a redeploy and a rename.
  • /AppStream/<name> - the readable form, which is what a person shares. It is resolved only when exactly one app holds that name; an ambiguous name answers 404 rather than guessing which app was meant.

A name a deploy states (streamServiceName in a compiled pack, name on the deploy routes) is the app's address as well as its label, so it has to be spellable as one URL segment: letters, digits, dot, dash, underscore or tilde, starting with a letter or digit, at most 64 characters, and not apps.json or index.html - which the App Stream answers itself. A publish that states anything else is refused with 400, and one that states a name another app already answers on is refused with 409, naming the folder that holds it.

A name derived from the folder carries no such rule: it is what a first publish that states no name gets, it is a label rather than an address, and two folders may share a leaf name. Such an app opens by id, or by name through percent-encoding when the name is unique. A later publish that states nothing inherits the name the app already has - stated or derived - so a deploy never renames an app back to its folder.

docs.title: One pack, either run time
docs.text: A SASjs Server runs programs as SAS or as JavaScript, chosen by RUN_TIMES. A deployment can carry both: the SAS service services/common/configure and the JS program services/common/configure.js sit side by side under the app's folder, and the run time decides which one runs. A pack built for a server that runs JS - the server target of a SASjs app with its JS mocks in serviceFolders - therefore works on either without a second build, and a browser-hosted site (which is a JS host) runs the same programs.

docs.title: Securing Apps
docs.text:
If you are running in "Server" mode you can grant permissions at the level of User or Group to any uploaded application - just click on your username, then "Settings", then "Permissions", to create the necessary rule(s).

An app's route names its ID, /AppStream/<id>, and the rule has to be written that way even when the URL a person opens shows the name (/app/<name>/): the permission is keyed on the id route, so a rule on /AppStream/macro-dash matches no route and grants nothing.
