docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
SASjs Server supports three authentication methods - Internal, LDAP, and OpenID Connect (OIDC).

These are selected with AUTH_PROVIDERS, which is a list - more than one may be enabled at once, for example LDAP for directory users together with OIDC for single sign-on.

Note that authentication is only available in server mode (not desktop).

docs.title: Internal Authentication
docs.text: By default, users are created using the internal database with a password configured by an admin. Groups can also be added, and permissions set against those groups.

docs.title: Disabling the local password login
docs.text:
Where every account lives in an identity provider, the internal password path can be switched off entirely: set LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED to false and a local account cannot sign in at all, because the stored password is never compared. LDAP-verified sign-in and the provider's own sign-in keep working. The login screen hides the password form while it is off, leaving the provider's button as the only way in.

This matters most where the app is reachable without a browser sign-in. On Cloudron the app package closes the local password path by default: with single sign-on configured and no break-glass admin seeded, no local account exists to use it, and /SASLogon/login is reachable from the internet - so an exposed password form would be the one credential an anonymous caller could guess.

docs.title: LDAP Authentication
docs.text:
SASjs Server can connect to an LDAP server (internally, we use the LDAPjs library). Any users / groups that are imported will be in addition to any internal users / groups. If there are conflicts, those particular users/groups will not be imported - to fix this, just delete the relevant (SASjs internal) users/groups and re-import.

Note that at least one internal admin user is necessary, to be able to log in and do the import. After this, the internal user may nominate other (LDAP) users as SASjs admins.

Configuration is made in the following .env settings:

AUTH_PROVIDERS=ldap
LDAP_URL= ldaps://LDAP_SERVER_URL:PORT
LDAP_BIND_DN= cn=admin,ou=system,dc=companyname
LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD = <password>
LDAP_USERS_BASE_DN = ou=users,dc=companyname
LDAP_GROUPS_BASE_DN = ou=groups,dc=companyname

Next, restart the server and log in with the admin user. Navigate to the settings tab. You should see a screen like the below. Import the users & groups by clicking the 'synchronise' button.

docs.title: OpenID Connect Authentication
docs.text:
SASjs Server can act as an OpenID Connect relying party, so users can sign in with any compliant provider (Okta, Entra ID, Keycloak, Google, Auth0, and so on). It is driven entirely by the provider's own discovery document, so no provider-specific code is involved - only configuration.

When OIDC is configured, a "Sign in with ..." button appears on the login screen automatically. The password form stays below it, so internal and LDAP users are unaffected - and a local admin can still sign in if the provider is unavailable.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
AUTH_PROVIDERS=oidc
OIDC_ISSUER_URL=https://id.example.com
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=sasjs-server
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<client secret>
OIDC_REDIRECT_URI=https://sas.example.com/SASLogon/openid/callback

The endpoints are then read from <OIDC_ISSUER_URL>/.well-known/openid-configuration. If your provider does not serve discovery at that path, supply it directly with OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL instead.

Register OIDC_REDIRECT_URI with your provider as the callback URL - the full URL, including the /SASLogon/openid/callback path. It must match exactly.

The remaining settings are optional and are listed under Settings.

docs.title: PKCE
docs.text:
Sign-in uses PKCE (RFC 7636) with the S256 challenge method: a per-attempt verifier is kept server-side, only its SHA-256 digest travels in the authorization request, and the code exchange sends the verifier - so a code intercepted in the browser cannot be redeemed by anything except the client instance that started the flow.

There is nothing to configure. The challenge is always sent, and your provider needs no extra registration for it; providers that require PKCE (some do, for confidential clients as well as public ones) are satisfied by it. It is also sent when the provider's discovery document does not advertise code_challenge_methods_supported - a provider that does not understand the parameter ignores it, whereas gating on that advertisement would be the downgrade the OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice warns about.

docs.title: How users are matched
docs.text:
The provider's sub claim is the durable identity. On each sign-in:

  1. The sub is looked up in the SASjs user table. A match signs that user in, regardless of what the username claim says.
  2. Otherwise, the username claim (preferred_username by default) is normalised to a SASjs username - lowercase, alphanumeric, up to 16 characters - and a user with that name is created, subject to the access policy below.
  3. If a user with that normalised name already exists and is not already linked to that provider account, the sign-in is refused rather than adopting the account. This is deliberate: the existing account may hold a local password and be an administrator. An admin must resolve the clash (rename one of the two) before that person can sign in.

docs.title: Access policy
docs.text:
Access is decided by the provider's groups claim, by fixed name:

Membership Result sasjs-admins signed in as a SASjs administrator sasjs-users signed in as an ordinary user neither refused, and no account is created

The names are not configurable. Membership is the whole access decision, so a deployment that could rename the groups could silently change who gets in. Membership is re-read on every sign-in, so removing someone from sasjs-admins demotes them the next time they sign in rather than leaving the elevation in place.

The groups scope is requested automatically when the provider's discovery document advertises it, and the claim is read from the id_token with a fallback to the provider's userinfo endpoint, because providers differ on where they put it.

Providers that cannot express groups (Google, for example) are exempt from the policy, and the first user to sign in becomes the administrator. Refusing every user of such a provider would be worse than granting one account, and the exemption is keyed on the discovery document, so it cannot be switched on by accident.

docs.title: Groups and permissions
docs.text:
Each sign-in mirrors the memberships the provider asserts onto SASjs groups of the same name, so a permission can be granted to a provider group rather than to each of its members in turn. The mirror is authoritative: a membership the provider stops asserting is removed at the next sign-in, so a revocation takes effect then rather than leaving the access the group granted in place.

Mirrored groups are marked as provider-managed, so their membership cannot be edited inside SASjs Server - it comes from the provider. A group name an administrator has already used locally, or one another provider owns, is left alone and reported in the server log rather than adopted: its members and the permissions pointing at it belong to whoever created it.

OpenID Connect reports the groups of the user who is signing in and offers no way to enumerate a directory, so this is a per-sign-in mirror rather than the bulk synchronisation LDAP allows. Permissions themselves are managed inside SASjs Server - see Authorisation.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text: The /SASLogon/openid/logout route clears the SASjs session and, when the provider advertises an end-session endpoint, redirects there so the single sign-on session is closed too.

docs.title: Example: Cloudron
docs.text:
Cloudron's user directory is an OIDC provider, and its addon exports the values you need. Map them onto the generic settings - no Cloudron-specific code is involved:

AUTH_PROVIDERS=oidc
OIDC_ISSUER_URL=$CLOUDRON_OIDC_ISSUER
OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL=$CLOUDRON_OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL
OIDC_CLIENT_ID=$CLOUDRON_OIDC_CLIENT_ID
OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=$CLOUDRON_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET
OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME=$CLOUDRON_OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME
OIDC_REDIRECT_URI=https://$CLOUDRON_APP_DOMAIN/SASLogon/openid/callback

and declare the callback in the app manifest:

"addons": {
  "oidc": {
    "loginRedirectUri": "/SASLogon/openid/callback",
    "logoutRedirectUri": "/",
    "tokenSignatureAlgorithm": "RS256"
  }
}

Cloudron asserts the username as the sub claim and sends group memberships in the groups claim, so a Cloudron user's group membership decides access as described above - create sasjs-users and sasjs-admins under Users > Groups and assign people to them. Those groups then appear inside the app as well, which is what lets you grant permissions to the group instead of user by user.

docs.title: Brute Force Protection
docs.text:
Failed password attempts are throttled by username. After MAX_LOGIN_FAILURES wrong passwords against one username, further attempts are refused with 429 Too Many Failed Attempts for LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MINUTES, whether or not the password is correct. A successful sign-in resets the counter.

The lockout is keyed on the username rather than the IP address: behind a reverse proxy every client shares the proxy's address, so an IP-keyed limit locks out the whole deployment rather than an attacker.

# failed attempts against one username before the login is refused
# default: 5
MAX_LOGIN_FAILURES = <number>

# how long the username stays locked out
# default: 15
LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MINUTES = <number>

Counters are held in process memory, so a server restart clears them. In the small, internal user base SASjs Server targets, a lockout is resolved by waiting out the window or asking an admin to restart.

docs.title: Admin Account
docs.text:
There is no default password, and no account exists until one is created. To seed a local admin, set ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL to a strong password; the account is named by ADMIN_USERNAME (default secretuser) and the password is in place until the first login.

In server mode the password is required unless an external auth provider is enabled: with a provider, leaving it unset seeds no local admin at all, and access is decided by the provider's groups - see Access policy.

If the admin password is misplaced, it can be reset by restarting the server with ADMIN_PASSWORD_RESET set to YES. Be sure to set it back to NO (or remove the option) to prevent the password being reset on any subsequent server restart.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text: SASjs Server runs in the foreground: it starts, binds its listeners and stays up until it receives SIGINT or SIGTERM. It does not daemonise, detach or write a pid file, so keeping it up is the job of whatever supervises the process. This page lists the options, what each one survives, and what a restart costs.

docs.title: Choosing a supervisor
docs.text:
Method Survives closing the terminal Restarts after a crash Starts at boot Platforms systemd yes yes yes Linux launchd yes yes at login macOS Task Scheduler yes yes, once configured at logon Windows WinSW, NSSM yes yes yes Windows pm2 yes yes yes Linux, macOS; Windows via pm2-installer nohup yes no no Linux, macOS foreground, npx no no no all

The recipes below assume the npm install (npm install -g @sasjs/server), so the command is sasjs-server. With the standalone executable, use its path instead: api-linux, api-macos or api-win.exe.

Do not run it as root. The server refuses to start as root unless RUN_AS is set to root deliberately.

docs.title: The working directory matters
docs.text: .env is read from the working directory, and sasjs_root - SAS WORK, the drive, the package cache and the logs - is created there. Every recipe below sets a working directory, and it should be a location that persists across restarts rather than, say, a user's home directory on a machine that is rebuilt.

docs.title: Linux: systemd
docs.text:
Write /etc/systemd/system/sasjs-server.service:

[Unit]
Description=SASjs Server
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
StartLimitIntervalSec=60
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=simple
User=sasjs
WorkingDirectory=/srv/sasjs
Environment=SAS_PATH=/opt/sas/sas.sh
EnvironmentFile=-/srv/sasjs/sasjs.env
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/sasjs-server
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

Then enable it and follow its log. The account and the directory must exist first, or the unit fails on start:

sudo useradd --system --home /srv/sasjs --shell /usr/sbin/nologin sasjs
sudo install -d -o sasjs -g sasjs /srv/sasjs
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now sasjs-server
journalctl -u sasjs-server -f
  • Restart=on-failure restarts a crashed process and leaves a deliberate systemctl stop alone, because the server exits 0 when it handles SIGTERM.
  • StartLimitIntervalSec and StartLimitBurst decide how many restarts systemd allows before it gives up. systemd's own default is five restarts in ten seconds; the values above allow five in a minute, so a transient failure still recovers while a wrong SAS_PATH - which exits with code 1 immediately - stops the unit instead of looping.
  • Environment= and EnvironmentFile= both win over an .env line with the same name, because dotenv does not overwrite variables that are already set.

docs.title: macOS: launchd
docs.text:
Write ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.sasjs.server.plist:

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>io.sasjs.server</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array><string>/usr/local/bin/sasjs-server</string></array>
  <key>WorkingDirectory</key><string>/Users/sasjs/server</string>
  <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
  <dict><key>SAS_PATH</key><string>/opt/sas/sas.sh</string></dict>
  <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
  <key>KeepAlive</key><true/>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/sasjs/server/logs/server.out</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/sasjs/server/logs/server.err</string>
</dict>
</plist>

Then load it:

mkdir -p /Users/sasjs/server/logs
launchctl bootstrap gui/$UID ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.sasjs.server.plist

launchctl bootout gui/$UID/io.sasjs.server removes it again; launchctl load -w works but is deprecated.

A LaunchAgent starts when that user logs in, and runs as that user. For a start before anyone logs in, install the same plist as a LaunchDaemon in /Library/LaunchDaemons (root-owned, and it needs a UserName key), which also means the server keeps running with nobody logged in.

docs.title: Windows: Task Scheduler
docs.text:
schtasks starts a task at logon, and that is all the command below configures: restart-on-failure is a task setting rather than a schtasks flag, so add it in the task's XML (<RestartOnFailure>) or in the Task Scheduler GUI under "If the task fails, restart every". Set the working directory explicitly, because a task's default working directory is C:\Windows\System32, which is where sasjs_root would otherwise be created:

schtasks /create /tn "SASjs Server" /sc onlogon /tr "cmd /c cd /d C:\sasjs && api-win.exe"

For a real Windows service - one that starts before anybody logs on - wrap the executable with WinSW or NSSM. With NSSM:

nssm install SASjsServer C:\sasjs\api-win.exe
nssm set SASjsServer AppDirectory C:\sasjs
nssm set SASjsServer AppStdout C:\sasjs\logs\server.out
nssm set SASjsServer AppStderr C:\sasjs\logs\server.err
nssm start SASjsServer

docs.title: pm2
docs.text:
pm2 is a process manager rather than an init system: it restarts what it manages, and hands the boot-time start to the platform.

pm2 start /usr/local/bin/sasjs-server --name sasjs-server
pm2 startup     # prints a command; run that command once
pm2 save        # records the current process list for the startup script

pm2 startup supports systemd, upstart and launchd. It does nothing on Windows, where the boot-time start needs pm2-installer, or Task Scheduler or a WinSW service. pm2 save is what makes the restart survive a reboot - without it the startup script starts an empty process list.

pm2 stops a process with SIGINT, which the server drains the same way as SIGTERM. pm2 logs --lines 200 shows the stderr that explains a crash.

docs.title: Foreground and nohup
docs.text:
nohup ./api-linux > server.log 2>&1 & disown

This survives closing the terminal, and nothing else: no restart after a crash, no start at boot, and the log is a file that nothing rotates.

docs.title: npx is a launcher, not a supervisor
docs.text:
npx @sasjs/server fetches the package and runs it in the foreground. When the terminal closes the process goes with it. Two things to know before using it:

  • A tag decides the version. Untagged, npx re-resolves latest on every start, so a restart silently changes version; pin the release you have tested in the install command.
  • The working directory still owns .env and sasjs_root, but the package itself lives in an evictable ~/.npm/_npx/<hash> cache, so an .env written next to the package would be lost.

For anything that has to stay up, install globally and give sasjs-server to the supervisor.

docs.title: Checking that it is up
docs.text:
GET /SASjsApi/info is public by design - the login screen needs the mode, the runtimes and the configured authentication providers before anyone has signed in - and it costs nothing:

curl -fsS http://localhost:5000/SASjsApi/info

A 200 with mode, httpPort/httpsPort and runTimes means the process is up and its listeners are bound. Use it as the probe in a monitoring script; systemd and Task Scheduler have no health check of their own.

docs.title: Why the process can stop
docs.text:
There are five ways out, and each has a distinct cause:

Situation Exit code Invalid environment at boot 1 No usable listener configuration 1 A listener cannot bind its port 1 SIGINT or SIGTERM 0 Unhandled promise rejection or uncaught exception 1 (the Node default)

The first three are configuration, and the log names the setting. The last one is the case where the stack trace is the diagnosis, so run the server where stderr is captured - the journal, pm2 logs, the task's output file - rather than in a console window that closes with the crash. Nothing in the server stops it because it has been idle.

docs.title: What a restart costs
docs.text:
• Sessions live in the server's memory, so a restart drops every session, ready or running. There is no session store to recover from.
  • A session is destroyed about 15 minutes after it is created, and a running one gets ten more minutes. Its folder is removed at that point.
  • SIGTERM and SIGINT drain in-flight HTTP requests for up to five seconds before the sockets are closed. A SAS process that is already running is a child of the server and is killed with it, so its log stops mid-program and the client sees the connection reset.
  • .env and the rest of the configuration are read at boot, so an edit takes effect on the next restart.

For work that runs longer than a request, submit a triggered program and poll it, so that the client is not holding a request open when the server restarts. Both routes require a bearer token outside desktop mode, which has no authentication at all:

# 1. Submit the program - the response carries the session id
SESSION_ID=$(curl -fsS -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  "http://localhost:5000/SASjsApi/stp/trigger?_program=/Public/app/run.sas" \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['sessionId'])")

# 2. Poll that id until the program finishes
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  "http://localhost:5000/SASjsApi/session/$SESSION_ID/state"
# -> {"state":"completed"}

# 3. Read what it produced, while the session is still alive
curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer ***" \
  "http://localhost:5000/SASjsApi/session/$SESSION_ID/log"

The state is an object, and the log and the output exist only for as long as the session does: see Sessions for the endpoints, the ownership rule and the retention window.

docs.title: Where can I learn more?
docs.text:
The following resources may be helpful:

  • Deploying SASjs Server on a VPS
  • Load Balancing with SASjs
  • Youtube playlist
  • Github: https://github.com/sasjs/server
  • RawSAS blog site

docs.title: Do I need a server?
docs.text: No! You can run SASjs Server on your laptop or computer - so long as you have a local instance of SAS.

docs.title: Will this work on SAS EBI?
docs.text: Yes - just point to the sas executable in the SASHOME folder

docs.title: Will this work with SAS University Edition
docs.text: No. If you are running University Edition, or the free / online learning instance, you cannot use SASjs. This is because there is no connectivity outside of these environments.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: There are two channels: the npm package and the standalone executable. Both read the same settings and serve the same API. Neither channel keeps the process running on its own: see Deployment for the ways to do that.

docs.title: npm
docs.text:
npx @sasjs/server

Or install it once and run sasjs-server from then on:

npm install -g @sasjs/server
sasjs-server

Requires Node 22 or later, and is the only channel that runs on arm64 (Apple Silicon, Graviton, a Pi) - the standalone executables are built for x64 only. Installing the package runs no install script, so it makes no network call of its own.

Run it from the directory the server should own: .env is read from the working directory, and that directory also gets ./sasjs_root. Without a tag, npx takes the latest release; for a deployment, pin the version in the install command to a release you have tested - they are listed on the npm page - because an untagged npx @sasjs/server re-resolves latest on every run, so a restart becomes a silent upgrade.

docs.title: Standalone executable
docs.text:
The latest version can be downloaded from the Releases page: https://github.com/sasjs/server/releases

On Linux it takes two lines:

curl -L https://github.com/sasjs/server/releases/latest/download/linux.zip > linux.zip
unzip linux.zip

macOS is the same package name changed: download macos.zip, and the executable inside is api-macos.

On Windows, download windows.zip and launch api-win.exe. You can ignore or cancel the popup; the app does not require administrative privileges.

The executables are built for x64 only. On arm64 - Apple Silicon, Graviton, a Raspberry Pi - use the npm package.

The executable unpacks the assets it serves into a tmp folder inside SASJS_ROOT, and removes it when the process exits, so nothing accumulates in the service account's home directory. See SASJS_ROOT to choose the location.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
After installation, there is only one mandatory input:

  • SAS_PATH -> the full path to the SAS executable (eg /path/to/sas.exe|sh) in your environment.

At least one listener must also be enabled, with HTTP_PORT, HTTPS_PORT or both. An environment that enables neither is refused at startup, with a message naming both variables.

There are many additional settings. They go in a file called .env in the directory the server runs from - for the executable, the folder holding api-linux / api-macos / api-win.exe:

SAS_PATH=/path/to/your/sas.sh
# This part enables multi-user SAS (optional)
MODE=server
DB_CONNECT=mongodb+srv://admin:***@cluster.mongodb.net/mydb?retryWrites=true&w=majority
# A plain HTTP listener, and a TLS listener beside it
HTTP_PORT=5000
HTTPS_PORT=8443
CERT_CHAIN=/opt/certificates/fullchain.pem
PRIVATE_KEY=/opt/certificates/privkey.pem

Ports below 1024 need the capability described under HTTP_PORT, which is why the sample uses 8443 for TLS; a deployment on 443 grants that capability to the executable instead.

Plain HTTP binds the loopback interface unless HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS names another one, and a non-loopback address is refused unless HTTP_ALLOW_REMOTE=true is set, because plain HTTP sends credentials in clear text.

Upgrading from a release that used the old listener settings takes one of two forms:

  • An install that set neither PROTOCOL nor PORT relied on the old default of plain HTTP on port 5000. It now enables no listener, so the server refuses to start and names both variables. Set HTTP_PORT=5000 before upgrading, or HTTPS_PORT with the certificate settings.
  • An install that ran with PROTOCOL=http and no HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS accepted connections on every interface. It now listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so a remote client gets connection refused until HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS names the interface you serve on and HTTP_ALLOW_REMOTE=true is set.

A PORT that is still in the file is translated into the matching listener for one release, with a warning, so an install that sets PORT alone keeps serving.

Then launch the executable (eg ./api-linux, or double click api-win.exe). The startup log states each listener as it binds - for example http on 127.0.0.1:5000 - and that address is the one to open.

There is also a guide to deploying SASjs Server on an Ubuntu VPS.

The server runs in the foreground. Deployment covers keeping it up with systemd, launchd, Task Scheduler or pm2.

docs.title: SSL Certificates
docs.text:
To run over https, SASjs server needs a copy of your certificates. The path to these certificates should be provided in the PRIVATE_KEY and CERT_CHAIN settings. If you are using self-signed certificates, then the CA_ROOT file should also be provided.

Example config:

HTTPS_PORT=443
CERT_CHAIN=/opt/certificates/fullchain.pem
PRIVATE_KEY=/opt/certificates/privkey.pem

Suggested instructions for obtaining certificates on a linux environment are provided below.

sudo snap install core; sudo snap refresh core
sudo snap install --classic certbot
sudo ln -s /snap/bin/certbot /usr/bin/certbot
# provide domain to prompt below WITHOUT https prefix, eg your.domain.com
sudo certbot certonly --standalone
# check for certificates
sudo ls /etc/letsencrypt/live/your.domain.com

For debugging certificate issues, the following link is useful: https://certbot.eff.org/instructions?ws=other&os=ubuntufocal

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions in SASjs are enabled when MODE=server. Rules do not apply to admin users. The menu is available under SETTINGS, and is divided into "URI Access" and "Folder Access". Rules can be at GROUP or USER level.

The hierarchy of rules is as follows:

  • By default, deny all
  • Apply group grants
  • Apply group deny
  • Apply user grants
  • Apply user deny

docs.title: URI Access
docs.text:
URI rules can be applied to the following endpoints:

  • /AppStream
  • /SASjsApi/code/execute
  • /SASjsApi/stp/execute
  • /SASjsApi/drive/deploy
  • /SASjsApi/drive/deploy/upload
  • /SASjsApi/drive/file
  • /SASjsApi/drive/folder
  • /SASjsApi/drive/fileTree
  • /SASjsApi/permission

They can also be applied to individual apps. This part of the list is dynamically generated, for example:

  • /AppStream/9f1c2d3e-4a5b-4c6d-8e7f-8a9b0c1d2e3f
  • /AppStream/2b7d4e1a-6c3f-4d8e-9a0b-1c2d3e4f5a6b

An app's route names its id, which is the last segment of its URL. A rule written before apps had an id names the app's label instead (/AppStream/Mario), and is still honoured: where a caller's rules speak about an id the id decides, and only when no rule names the id does the label decide.

docs.title: Folder Access
docs.text: Coming soon.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session occurs in a session folder, and may be executed using either a SAS or a JS runtime. The session folder will contain any uploaded files, as well as the program / script being executed (prepended with code to enable relevant variables, such as URL parameters).

The program itself will write the output to _webout, setting the header properties in a file, the location of which is in the sasjs_stpsrv_header_loc variable.

docs.title: SAS Runtime
docs.text:
In triggering the SAS executable, there are two factors that need to be overcome:

  1. The process is expensive to launch (startup cost)
  2. Once launched, the process will run until the end and cannot be 'communicated' with directly

To improve responsiveness, it is critical to prelaunch SAS sessions. But how to provide an arbitrary SAS program to a running SAS session (without impacting the session itself)?

The solution, was to take the following steps:

  1. Launch SAS with an autoexec and a dummy program (SAS won't start without SYSIN)
  2. Delete the dummy file in the autoexec, then loop until the "real" program appears

The actual SAS code used for this:

data _null_;
  /* remove the dummy SYSIN */
  length fname $8;
  rc=filename(fname,getoption('SYSIN') );
  if rc=0 and fexist(fname) then rc=fdelete(fname);
  rc=filename(fname);
  /* now wait for the real SYSIN */
  slept=0;
  do until ( fileexist(getoption('SYSIN')) or slept>(60*15) );
    /* check every 100ms if the file exists yet */
    slept=slept+sleep(0.1,1);
  end;
run;

With this loop in place, SASjs Server can prespawn a SAS session and wait until a request arrives. It will then perform the following in parallel:

  1. Spawn a new session (ready for the next request)
  2. Inject the _PROGRAM code into an existing (HOT) session

This is a simplistic overview. In reality it's a bit more complicated as we need to create a unique folder for each session, keep track of the sessions, and ensure we don't launch a session that is just about to expire. We also need to work across multiple threads.

The full process flow is therefore as follows:

docs.title: JS Runtime
docs.text: JS sessions are not pre-spawned, as NodeJS is already running. URL variables are injected into the beginning of the program as constants.

docs.title: Reading a session's results
docs.text:
A triggered program keeps running after the trigger call returns, so the results are fetched from the session rather than from a response body. Three endpoints serve them while the session is alive:

Endpoint Returns GET /SASjsApi/session/{sessionId}/log the program's log, as text/plain GET /SASjsApi/session/{sessionId}/output its _webout, with the content type the program set in stpsrv_header.txt GET /SASjsApi/session/{sessionId} the session itself: state, pid while it runs, timestamps, failureReason, and the retention window

GET /SASjsApi/session/{sessionId}/state answers an object rather than a bare string:

{ "state": "running" }

That is the shape a Viya caller already polls from the compute API, so a client can be written once for both. The states are initialising, pending, running, completed and failed.

An empty log body is not the same as a missing one. Empty means the program has not written anything yet, while a 404 means the session no longer exists - which is what an expired session answers, because there is nothing left to read.

Each session belongs to the user that created it, recorded when the session is made. The log, the output and the details are served to that user, or to an administrator; anyone else receives a 404, because a session id is guessable and confirming it would confirm the guess. In desktop mode the single fixed local user owns every session.

Results outlive the session for a limited time. expiresAfterMins on the trigger call asks to keep them that many minutes past completion; without it the folder is removed about 15 minutes after creation. A session id is therefore not a durable handle - fetch the log before the window closes, or copy it somewhere the server does not manage.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
All settings in SASjs server are made by means of environment variables. These can be set in the following places:

  • Configured globally in /etc/environment file
  • Export in terminal or shell script (export VAR=VALUE)
  • Prepended in the command
  • Enter in the .env file alongside the executable

The usual / preferred method is to provide the variables in the .env file (which works on both Windows & Linux) as follows:

In a server environment, it is highly recommended to protect this file with appropriate permissions (eg, to prevent changes being made by the shared identity under which the server is launched)

docs.title: ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL
docs.text:
Defines the initial (temporary) password for the ADMIN_USERNAME, which is in place until the first login. There is no default: a default would ship a publicly-known credential. In server mode it is required unless an external auth provider is enabled - with a provider, leaving it unset seeds no local admin at all, and access is decided by the provider's groups - see Access policy.

Example:

ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL=<a strong password>

docs.title: ADMIN_PASSWORD_RESET
docs.text:
This option can be used to force a reset of the password of the ADMIN_USERNAME. Default is NO. Possible options are YES and NO. If ADMIN_PASSWORD_RESET=YES then the ADMIN_USERNAME will be prompted to change the password from ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL on next login. This will repeat on every server restart, unless the option is removed / set to NO.

If the ADMIN_USERNAME is an existing, non-admin user then the password will NOT be reset (only works for admins). If the ADMIN_USERNAME uses an auth provider (eg LDAP) then again, this approach will not work. In this case, you can create a new admin user by setting a new ADMIN_USERNAME.

Example: 

ADMIN_PASSWORD_RESET=NO

docs.title: ADMIN_USERNAME
docs.text:
Used to define the name of the local admin user. The default value is secretuser. The user is created on startup only when ADMIN_PASSWORD_INITIAL is set.

Example:

ADMIN_USERNAME=secretuser

docs.title: AUTH_PROVIDERS
docs.text:
Used to list the desired Authentication providers (space or comma separated). Supported values are ldap and oidc, and more than one may be enabled at once - for example LDAP for directory users together with OpenID Connect for single sign-on. See Authentication for the detail of each.

Example: 

AUTH_PROVIDERS=ldap

Combining providers: 

AUTH_PROVIDERS=ldap oidc

docs.title: ALLOWED_DOMAIN
docs.text:
Prevent authentication from other domains by listing the primary domain here. This will reject cookies arriving from any other domain. Used only when MODE=server, and only relevant for SASjs Studio / SASjs Logon.

Example: 

ALLOWED_DOMAIN=sas.company.com

For API use by different servers / domains, see CORS and WHITELIST settings.

docs.title: API_SERVER_URL
docs.text:
The URL generated stored programs use to call back into this server. Unset, it is taken from the request that starts the session; set it when that is wrong for the topology - behind a reverse proxy or a load balancer, for instance - because the value is written into each program verbatim, so a wrong one only surfaces when the program runs. It must be an http(s) URL with no path: https://host is accepted and https://host/base is refused, so a deployment behind a path-prefixed proxy has to set the value some other way. A value with a path is refused at startup, while the configuration is still in front of you. (The check does not look past the host, so a query or fragment passes it - no program needs one.)

Example:

API_SERVER_URL=https://sas.4gl.io

docs.title: CERT_CHAIN
docs.text:
Necessary when HTTPS_PORT is set.

Example: CERT_CHAIN=localhost.crt

See also:

  • HTTPS_PORT
  • CA_ROOT
  • PRIVATE_KEY

Developer notes: processed internally as cert: option which has this description:

Cert chains in PEM format. One cert chain should be provided per private key. Each cert chain should consist of the PEM formatted certificate for a provided private key, followed by the PEM formatted intermediate certificates (if any), in order, and not including the root CA (the root CA must be pre-known to the peer, see ca). When providing multiple cert chains, they do not have to be in the same order as their private keys in key. If the intermediate certificates are not provided, the peer will not be able to validate the certificate, and the handshake will fail.

docs.title: CA_ROOT
docs.text:
Necessary when HTTPS_PORT is set AND the server uses a self-signed certificate.

Example: CA_ROOT=fullchain.pem

See also:

  • HTTPS_PORT
  • PRIVATE_KEY
  • CERT_CHAIN

Developer notes: processed internally as ca: option which has this description:

Optionally override the trusted CA certificates. Default is to trust the well-known CAs curated by Mozilla. Mozilla's CAs are completely replaced when CAs are explicitly specified using this option. The value can be a string or Buffer, or an Array of strings and/or Buffers. Any string or Buffer can contain multiple PEM CAs concatenated together. The peer's certificate must be chainable to a CA trusted by the server for the connection to be authenticated. When using certificates that are not chainable to a well-known CA, the certificate's CA must be explicitly specified as a trusted or the connection will fail to authenticate. If the peer uses a certificate that doesn't match or chain to one of the default CAs, use the ca option to provide a CA certificate that the peer's certificate can match or chain to. For self-signed certificates, the certificate is its own CA, and must be provided. For PEM encoded certificates, supported types are "TRUSTED CERTIFICATE", "X509 CERTIFICATE", and "CERTIFICATE". See also tls.rootCertificates.

docs.title: CORS
docs.text:
Options: [disable|enable]

Default: disable for server & enable for desktop

If enabled, it is also necessary to configure the WHITELIST of additional server(s).

docs.title: DB_CONNECT
docs.text:
In server mode it is necessary to use a database to store a number of attributes, such as:

  • Users & Groups (if not using LDAP or other authentication source)
  • Clients / Secrets (to enable REST API connections)
  • Private keys (to spawn client ids, session tokens etc)
  • Permissions (which users / groups are authorised to access which resources)

This value contains the Connection string for the DB instance. Example: 

DB_CONNECT=mongodb+srv://<DB_USERNAME>:<DB_PASSWORD>@<CLUSTER>/<DB_NAME>?retryWrites=true&w=majority
See also:

  • DB_TYPE

docs.title: DB_TYPE
docs.text:
Specify the type of database. When DB_TYPE=cosmos_mongodb the connection is made using compatibility mode.

Options: [mongodb|cosmos_mongodb]

Default: mongodb

docs.title: DDC_HOST_ENABLED
docs.text:
Serves a development page at /ddc-host that embeds an application the way SAS Visual Analytics embeds data-driven content: an iframe carrying VA's sandbox attribute set, and a message posted into it on a chosen timing. Use it to check that an embedded application works inside that sandbox, which opening it as a top-level page does not exercise. The page and its script are both served behind this setting.

Options: [YES|NO]

Default: NO. The page frames whatever URL it is given, so it belongs on a development server rather than on one a browser user can reach.

Example:

DDC_HOST_ENABLED=YES

See also:

  • Testing VA embedding

docs.title: DRIVE_LOCATION
docs.text:
This setting is useful if you are running multiple instances of SASjs Server and would like to re-use the same Drive folder, Macros, Packages, and appStream config.

The DRIVE_LOCATION can be shared across instances, but the SASJS_ROOT can't - as it will cause conflicts with sessions / uploads etc.

If using this feature, be aware that the index of published apps (appStreamConfig.json, in the drive folder) is read at server startup and refreshed when an instance publishes or removes an app - so a deploy made on one instance reaches the others on their next restart. If this is problematic for your project, please raise an issue.

See also:

  • LOG_LOCATION
  • SASJS_ROOT

docs.title: HELMET_COEP
docs.text:
HELMET Cross Origin Embedder Policy. Sets the Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy header to require-corp when true

Options: [true|false]

Default: true

Docs: https://helmetjs.github.io/#reference (crossOriginEmbedderPolicy)

docs.title: HELMET_CSP_CONFIG_PATH
docs.text:
HELMET Content Security Policy

Path to a json file containing HELMET contentSecurityPolicy directives

The default policy allows no inline scripts and no inline event handlers, so a script injected into a page the server serves cannot run. The style-src directive is untouched by this default and keeps 'unsafe-inline', which the styling libraries used by the web interface require.

An application deployed on the server that needs inline scripts or inline event handlers (many Angular and Data Controller builds do) loosens the policy with its own config file.

Docs: https://helmetjs.github.io/#reference

Default config: 

{
  "frame-src": ["'self'"],
  "img-src": ["'self'", "data:", "blob:"],
  "script-src": ["'self'"],
  "script-src-attr": ["'none'"]
}

Loosened config for an app that requires inline scripts: 

{
  "frame-src": ["'self'"],
  "img-src": ["'self'", "data:", "blob:"],
  "script-src": ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"],
  "script-src-attr": ["'self'", "'unsafe-inline'"]
}

Example: HELMET_CSP_CONFIG_PATH=./csp.config.json

The policy actually sent when the variable is unset: helmet's own defaults, in the order helmet writes them, with the directives this server adds.

default-src 'self'
base-uri 'self'
font-src 'self' https: data:
form-action 'self'
frame-ancestors 'self'
img-src 'self' data: blob:
object-src 'none'
script-src 'self'
script-src-attr 'none'
style-src 'self' https: 'unsafe-inline'
upgrade-insecure-requests
  • blob: in img-src is what lets the Studio draw a drive image: it fetches the file and hands the page an object URL, which a policy without blob: refuses - the preview pane is then simply empty.
  • script-src 'self' with script-src-attr 'none' is the reason a script injected into a page the server serves cannot run: there is no 'unsafe-inline', and inline event handlers are refused. An application that needs them opts in through the config file above.
  • style-src keeps 'unsafe-inline' because the styling libraries the interface uses emit inline style attributes; it is not a licence for inline scripts.
  • upgrade-insecure-requests is dropped when the request arrived on the plain HTTP listener, where rewriting subresources to https:// breaks every one of them.
  • frame-ancestors 'self' keeps other sites from framing the server; form-action 'self' keeps a form on a page from posting elsewhere.

docs.title: HTTP_ALLOW_REMOTE
docs.text:
Required to bind the plain HTTP listener to an address that is not loopback. Plain HTTP sends credentials in clear text, so a non-loopback HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS is refused unless this is true.

Options: [true|false]

Default: unset (refused)

HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0
HTTP_ALLOW_REMOTE=true

docs.title: HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS
docs.text:
The interface the plain HTTP listener binds to.

Default: 127.0.0.1

See also: HTTP_ALLOW_REMOTE

docs.title: HTTP_PORT
docs.text:
Port for the plain HTTP listener. Setting it enables the listener; unset, empty and 0 all leave it disabled. HTTP_PORT and HTTPS_PORT may be used alone or together, and at least one must be set or the server refuses to start. The two must also differ - two listeners cannot share a port.

Default: unset (listener disabled)

Binding to a port below 1024 needs privileges, so grant the capability to the executable rather than running SASjs Server under a privileged account: setcap 'cap_net_bind_service=+ep' /home/sasjssrv/api-linux. Run it again after replacing the executable.

See also: HTTPS_PORT, HTTP_BIND_ADDRESS

docs.title: HTTPS_BIND_ADDRESS
docs.text:
The interface the TLS listener binds to. Unset, the listener binds every interface.

See also: HTTPS_PORT

docs.title: HTTPS_PORT
docs.text:
Port for the TLS listener. Setting it enables the listener; unset, empty and 0 all leave it disabled, the same rule as HTTP_PORT. It requires CERT_CHAIN and PRIVATE_KEY.

Binding this listener to a port below 1024 needs the same capability the HTTP_PORT note describes, and TLS on 443 is the common case for it - grant the capability to the executable rather than running the server as root.

Default: unset (listener disabled)

See also: HTTP_PORT, HTTPS_BIND_ADDRESS

docs.title: LDAP_URL
docs.text:
The URL of the LDAP directory server.

Example: 

LDAP_URL= ldaps://LDAP_SERVER_URL:PORT

docs.title: LDAP_BIND_DN
docs.text:
Example: 

LDAP_BIND_DN=cn=admin,ou=system,dc=companyname

docs.title: LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD
docs.text:
All LDAP queries have to be authenticated with this secret and the LDAP_USERS_BASE_DN

Example: 

LDAP_BIND_PASSWORD = <password>

docs.title: LDAP_USERS_BASE_DN
docs.text: LDAP_USERS_BASE_DN = ou=users,dc=companyname

docs.title: LDAP_GROUPS_BASE_DN
docs.text: LDAP_GROUPS_BASE_DN = ou=groups,dc=companyname

docs.title: LOCAL_LOGIN_ENABLED
docs.text:
Whether a local (database) account can sign in with its stored password. Set to false and the password is never compared, so a local account cannot sign in at all - useful where every account lives in an identity provider instead. On the Cloudron app package this defaults to false when single sign-on is configured and no break-glass admin is seeded.

The login screen follows it: with local sign-in off the password form is hidden, so a deployment that signs everyone in through a provider shows the provider's button alone.

Accounts that authenticate through LDAP are unaffected: their password is verified against the directory. OIDC users sign in through the provider.

It cannot be false while AUTH_PROVIDERS is empty - with the local login gone and no provider to authenticate against, no account could sign in, so the server refuses to start rather than run unreachable.

Options: [true|false]

Default: true

docs.title: LOG_FORMAT_MORGAN
docs.text:
These setting determines the level of logging produced by SASjs server. More details on this can be found in the Morgan documentation here:https://www.npmjs.com/package/morgan#predefined-formats

Options: [combined|common|dev|short|tiny]

Default: common

docs.title: LOG_LOCATION
docs.text:
Location in which to write server logs (one file per day). If not provided, logs are written in a /logs subfolder of the SASJS_ROOT location. Can be a full path, else relative to the directory in which the server instance was launched. More information on the behaviour (eg log rotation) is available in the underlying package (rotating-file-stream).

Example: LOG_LOCATION=./sasjs_root/logs

docs.title: LOGIN_LOCKOUT_MINUTES
docs.text:
How long a username stays locked out after MAX_LOGIN_FAILURES failed password attempts. The lockout is keyed on the username, not the IP address: behind a reverse proxy every client shares one address, so an IP-keyed limit would lock out the whole deployment rather than an attacker.

Default: 15

docs.title: MAX_LOGIN_FAILURES
docs.text:
Failed password attempts against one username before the login is refused with 429 Too Many Failed Attempts. Counters reset when the username signs in successfully.

Default: 5

docs.title: MOCK_SERVERTYPE
docs.text:
Used internally for CLI / Adapter testing - set to SAS9 or SASVIYA when launching to enable responses in the format of alternative platforms. These mocks are not functional, and have no use outside of development / testing purposes.

Default: SASJS

docs.title: MODE
docs.text:
Whether to launch the server in desktop (single user / workstation) or server mode (multi-user). For server mode, a Mongo DB connection string must be provided in the DB_CONNECT variable.

Default: desktop

docs.title: NODE_PATH
docs.text:
The path to the NodeJS executable (for running JavaScript programs).

Example: NODE_PATH=~/.nvm/versions/node/v16.14.0/bin/node

See also:

  • PYTHON_PATH
  • RUN_TIMES
  • SAS_PATH

docs.title: OIDC_ISSUER_URL
docs.text:
The issuer URL of your OpenID Connect provider. SASjs Server reads the provider's endpoints from <OIDC_ISSUER_URL>/.well-known/openid-configuration. Required when oidc is listed in AUTH_PROVIDERS, unless OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL is given instead.

Example: 

OIDC_ISSUER_URL=https://id.example.com

docs.title: OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL
docs.text:
Use this instead of OIDC_ISSUER_URL when your provider does not serve its discovery document at the conventional path. Optional.

Example: 

OIDC_DISCOVERY_URL=https://id.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

docs.title: OIDC_CLIENT_ID
docs.text:
The client ID issued by your provider for SASjs Server. Required when oidc is listed in AUTH_PROVIDERS.

Example: 

OIDC_CLIENT_ID=sasjs-server

docs.title: OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET
docs.text:
The client secret issued by your provider. Required when oidc is listed in AUTH_PROVIDERS.

This value is write-only: it is read from the environment and used, but it is never returned by the API or shown in the settings screen.

Example: 

OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET=<client secret>

docs.title: OIDC_REDIRECT_URI
docs.text:
The callback URL, which must be registered with your provider and must match exactly. Required when oidc is listed in AUTH_PROVIDERS. It must be an absolute http or https URL, and the path is fixed by the server.

Example: 

OIDC_REDIRECT_URI=https://sas.example.com/SASLogon/openid/callback

docs.title: OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME
docs.text:
The label shown on the sign-in button, as in "Sign in with ". Defaults to OpenID Connect.

Example: 

OIDC_PROVIDER_NAME=Example Identity

docs.title: OIDC_SCOPE
docs.text:
The scopes requested from the provider. Defaults to openid profile email, and must always include openid.

Example: 

OIDC_SCOPE=openid profile email

docs.title: OIDC_USERNAME_CLAIM
docs.text:
The claim used to derive the SASjs username when provisioning a new user. Defaults to preferred_username, falling back to sub when the claim is absent. The value is normalised to a SASjs username - lowercase, alphanumeric, up to 16 characters.

Example: 

OIDC_USERNAME_CLAIM=email

docs.title: OIDC_SIGNING_ALG
docs.text:
The algorithm used to verify the provider's id_token signature. Defaults to RS256. Valid options are RS256, RS384, RS512, ES256, ES384, ES512 and EdDSA. Set this to match what your provider signs with.

Example: 

OIDC_SIGNING_ALG=RS256

docs.title: OIDC_JIT_PROVISION
docs.text:
Whether a user who signs in successfully but has no SASjs account should have one created automatically. Defaults to true. Set to false to require that an admin creates the account first. The new account's administrator status comes from the provider's groups, as described under Access policy.

Example: 

OIDC_JIT_PROVISION=true

docs.title: OIDC_POST_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URI
docs.text:
Where the provider should send the browser after the single sign-on session is closed. Optional - when omitted, logout returns to the SASjs Server home page.

Example: 

OIDC_POST_LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URI=https://sas.example.com/

docs.title: PORT
docs.text: Deprecated - use HTTP_PORT or HTTPS_PORT. For one release PORT and PROTOCOL are translated into the matching port variable, with a warning, and are removed after that. An environment that sets HTTP_PORT or HTTPS_PORT ignores both, and the warning says so.

docs.title: PRIVATE_KEY
docs.text:
Necessary when HTTPS_PORT is set.

Example: PRIVATE_KEY=localhost.key

See also:

  • HTTPS_PORT
  • CA_ROOT
  • CERT_CHAIN

Developer notes: processed internally as key: option which has this description:

Private keys in PEM format. PEM allows the option of private keys being encrypted. Encrypted keys will be decrypted with options.passphrase. Multiple keys using different algorithms can be provided either as an array of unencrypted key strings or buffers, or an array of objects in the form {pem: [, passphrase: ]}. The object form can only occur in an array. object.passphrase is optional. Encrypted keys will be decrypted with object.passphrase if provided, or options.passphrase if it is not.

docs.title: PROTOCOL
docs.text:
Deprecated - the listeners a deployment serves are stated by HTTP_PORT and HTTPS_PORT, each of which enables its own listener. For one release PROTOCOL and PORT are translated into the matching port variable, with a warning, and are removed after that.

If using https (strongly recommended), the following items should also be configured:

  • ALLOWED_DOMAIN
  • CA_ROOT
  • CERT_CHAIN
  • PRIVATE_KEY

docs.title: PYTHON_PATH
docs.text:
The path to the Python executable (for running Python programs).

Example: PYTHON_PATH=/usr/bin/python

See also:

  • NODE_PATH
  • R_PATH
  • RUN_TIMES
  • SAS_PATH

docs.title: R_PATH
docs.text:
The path to the R executable (for running R programs). Installation guides for R are available for Centos 7, ubuntu and Debian.

Example: R_PATH=/usr/bin/Rscript

  • NODE_PATH
  • PYTHON_PATH
  • RUN_TIMES
  • SAS_PATH

docs.title: RUN_AS
docs.text:
The account the server must run as.

Unset, the server refuses to start as root. Set to a username, the server refuses to start as any other account, so the value asserts where it runs rather than suggesting it. RUN_AS=root is the deliberate override.

The server executes uploaded code by design, so the identity it runs under is the privilege every connected user gets - and in desktop mode there is no authentication at all. Start it under the account that should own the SAS sessions, rather than with sudo.

The check runs at startup, before any listener binds and before the working directory and sasjs_root are set up, so a refused start leaves nothing behind.

Default: unset (root refused)

See also: Deployment

docs.title: RUN_TIMES
docs.text:
A comma separated string that defines the available runtimes.

Priority is given to the runtime that comes first in the string.

Given a RUNTIME=js,sas,py:

  • If _program=/some/program then SASjs Server will first look for program.js in the /some folder, then program.sas, and finally program.py.
  • If _program=/some/program.sas then a SAS runtime will always be used.
  • If _program=/some/program.r then an R runtime will be used (and so-on)

Supported runtimes:

  • js - JavaScript
  • sas - SAS
  • py - Python
  • r - R

Default: sas,js,py

Example:

RUN_TIMES=js,sas,py

docs.title: SAS_PATH
docs.text:
The full path to the SAS executable (sas.exe / sas.sh). It is highly recommended to provide an instance with UTF-8 encoding, for the following reasons:

  • SASjs Adapter compatibility
  • Broad language support
  • Viya compatibility

To force UTF-8 encoding, update the appropriate sasv9.cfg file with the following option:

-ENCODING UTF-8

Example:

SAS_PATH=/path/to/sas/executable.exe

See also:

  • NODE_PATH
  • PYTHON_PATH
  • RUN_TIMES

docs.title: SASJS_ROOT
docs.text:
If omitted, this will be the SASjs Server installation directory. The location is used for SAS WORK, staged files, DRIVE, configuration etc

A standalone executable also unpacks the assets it serves into a tmp subfolder here, and removes it when the process exits. A start also removes leftover folders from earlier runs once they are a day old, so a process that was killed does not leave one behind for good.

Example:

SASJS_ROOT=./sasjs_root

docs.title: SITE_ID
docs.text:
The site that stored programs report as SYSSITE. A SAS session sets that macro variable itself, but a program running in the JavaScript runtime has none, so the value comes from this server's configuration. Default 123, the SASjs demonstration site. Unset, or blank, leaves it undefined and the default applies.

Example:

SITE_ID=123

docs.title: STATIC_MOCK_LOCATION
docs.text:
The folder the SAS 9 mock reads its files from and writes uploads into - the routes that stand in for /SASStoredProcess and the pages around it. A relative path is resolved against the working directory; an absolute path is used as written. Default mocks.

Example:

STATIC_MOCK_LOCATION=mocks

docs.title: WHITELIST
docs.text:
The browser origins that may call the server cross-origin, comma or space separated. Each entry is an origin - scheme, host and port only, with no path, query or trailing slash:

WHITELIST=http://localhost:3000,https://abc.com

A browser sends an Origin header that is a bare origin, so an entry carrying a path or a query can never match a request. The server refuses to start rather than register an allow-list entry that would answer nobody.

See also:

  • CORS

docs.title: Stored Programs
docs.text:
Stored Programs may be written in SAS, Python, R, or JavaScript and are saved to SASjs Drive. When the /SASjsApi/stp/execute endpoint is called with a _PROGRAM URL parameter (pointing to the logical program location), a "Stored Program" is prepared and executed in a SAS/JS/PYTHON/R session according to the file extension.

For the usual case where the _program variable does NOT contain an extension (eg /some/stored/program) then by default, SASjs Server will attempt to find "program.sas" in the /some/stored folder. To change this default, see the RUN_TIMES settings.

When Stored Programs are executed, some pre-code is injected to make available various inputs, such as:

  • Input Macro Variables
  • Input Files
  • Utility Macros / Functions

The implementation varies depending on whether it is running as a SAS, JS, Python or R session.

If you are calling your Stored Programs from a web application, it is recommended to review the sasjs/adapter (designed to work with Stored Programs) and associated seed apps. You might also want to review the Data Controller source as an example of a relatively large, commercial application built on SASjs.

docs.title: Special Variables
docs.text: The following variables are "special":

docs.title: _PROGRAM
docs.text: This is a required input, and will point to the Stored Program location in SASjs Drive. The extension may be omitted, subject to the behaviour in the RUN_TIMES setting.

docs.title: _DEBUG
docs.text:
Setting this to 131 or greater will result in the log being returned. The log is framed by the following UUID: SASJS_LOGS_SEPARATOR_163ee17b6ff24f028928972d80a26784

The log can itself contain that UUID - a program's source is echoed into its log, so the literal appears wherever ms_runstp or ms_testservice is part of the submitted code, and a service that calls another puts the nested response in it. The framing adds exactly two occurrences, one either side of the log: webout is everything before the first, the log everything between the first and the last, and the print output what follows the last. That holds while webout and the print output carry no occurrence of their own - neither is anything the server adds, though a program that echoes another response into _webout can put one there.

Setting _DEBUG also results in the creation of a Content-Type header of text/plain.

docs.title: Input Variables
docs.text:
Any URL parameters (eg &name1=value1&something=else) are attached as macro variables eg as follows:

%let name1=value1;
%let something=else;

A number of "fixed" variables are also added at the start of the program - the code that generates them is in the repo, in the program template in Execution.ts.

If _DEBUG is set then options mprint; will also be automatically added to the start of the Stored Program.

docs.title: Input Files
docs.text:
Any files attached to a request will be saved in the session folder and the following variables will be dynamically added to the SAS program:

  • _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT - contains an integer, from 0 to the number of files to being provided. This variable is always created.
  • _WEBIN_FILENAME1 - the value that was specified in the FILENAME attribute by the frontend
  • _WEBIN_FILEREF1 - An 8 letter code, starting with an underscore and finishing with 7 random alphanumeric characters
  • _WEBIN_NAME1 - the value that was specified in the NAME attribute by the frontend

We will also create the fileref(s) using the filename statement.

To illustrate with an example - we are uploading two files, F1 and F2. The following SAS code will be generated, and inserted at the beginning of the executed program:

/* request files */
filename _SJS0001 "/some/temp/location/file1";
filename _SJS0002 "/some/temp/location/file2";
%let _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT=2;
%let _WEBIN_FILENAME1=myfile.csv;
%let _WEBIN_FILENAME2=myotherfile.txt;
%let _WEBIN_FILEREF1=_SJS0001;
%let _WEBIN_FILEREF2=_SJS0002;
%let _WEBIN_NAME1=F1;
%let _WEBIN_NAME2=F2;

If there are no files uploaded, only the following code will be generated:

/* request files */
%let _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT=0;

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Any response data should be written to the _webout fileref (which is pre-assigned in the session). The corresponding header records (content type etc) can be written using the mfs_httpheader macro. Additional SASjs Server specific macros are also available.

The response (content and header) will vary depending on the _debug setting.

docs.title: JS Programs
docs.text:
The use of JS "programs" as your backend is highly beneficial for the following use cases:

  • You would like to test your application in a non SAS environment (such as a CI/CD pipeline or developer machine)
  • You would like to make use of JS packages in your backend SAS applications
  • You would like to provide backup services in the case that SAS is down (eg licence expiry)

Any console.log() statements written by your JavaScript will be returned in the response "log" (identically to SAS).

If your Job / Service / Test depends on any third party libraries / packages, then you need to bundle that service before deploying it to sasjs server. You can choose any bundler for this process. One possible option could be webpack. If you choose webpack then you can use it like this:

npx webpack --mode none --target node --entry <path-of-file-to-bundle/build> --output-path <path-of-output-folder> --output-filename <name-of-output-file>

For instance if you have a mock service at path sasjs/services/common/appinit.js and you want to build and make it ready for deployment, you can run the following in the terminal:

npx webpack --mode none --target node --entry ./sasjs/services/common/appinit.js --output-path sasjsbuild/services/common --output-filename appinit.js

Repeat this for any other JS Stored Programs as needed.

Finally, run sasjs build to create the deployment pack, and sasjs deploy to deploy.

docs.title: Input Variables
docs.text:
Any URL parameters (eg &name1=value1&something=else) are attached as JS variables eg as follows:

const name1='value1'
const something='else'

A JS program is generated in six parts - the host's fs, your request parameters, the runtime variables, the webout() block, your program, and a closing statement. This is the shape, with the paths of one session:

globalThis.fs = require('fs')

/* runtime vars */
const _program = '/Public/app/myprogram';
const _debug = '';

/* dynamic user-provided vars */
let _webout = '';
const weboutPath = '/home/sasjssrv/sasjs_root/sessions/20220808081136-29012-1659946296436/webout.txt';
const _SASJS_TOKENFILE = '/home/sasjssrv/sasjs_root/sessions/20220808081136-29012-1659946296436/reqHeaders.txt';
const _SASJS_WEBOUT_HEADERS = '/home/sasjssrv/sasjs_root/sessions/20220808081136-29012-1659946296436/stpsrv_header.txt';
const _SASJS_APISERVERURL = 'http://127.0.0.1:5000';
const _SASJS_USERNAME = 'allan';
const _SASJS_USERID = '6';
const _SASJS_DISPLAYNAME = 'Allan Bowe';
const _METAPERSON = _SASJS_DISPLAYNAME;
const _METAUSER = _SASJS_USERNAME;
const SASJSPROCESSMODE = 'Stored Program';

/* webout(): send data back, mirroring %ms_webout in @sasjs/core.
   webout('OPEN'); webout('OBJ', 'name', rows); webout('CLOSE')
   Generated by @sasjs/utils - change it there, not here. */
const _sasjs_webout_config = { ... }
/* ...and the rest of the block, see "Output" below */
globalThis.webout = _sasjs_webout;

/* actual job code */
// your program

/* the tail, which writes _webout if your program assigned it */
_sasjs_webout.finalise(_webout)

fs and webout are published as globals, so a program that declares its own fs or webout shadows it without clashing with the runtime's. The runtime keeps its own reference under the reserved _sasjs_webout name, which is also what writes _webout when the program assigns that variable instead of calling webout().

webout() is generated into the program rather than imported, from the single copy of the block in @sasjs/utils: the server and sasjs mock emit the same text, so a program behaves the same in both, and the session log shows exactly what ran. The block resolves its own fs (and os, when the host has one, falling back to what a browser can answer).

docs.title: Input Files
docs.text:
Any files attached to a request will be saved in the session folder and the following variables will be dynamically added to the JS program:

  • _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT - contains an integer, from 0 to the number of files to being provided. This variable is always created.
  • _WEBIN_FILENAME1 - the value that was specified in the FILENAME attribute by the frontend
  • _WEBIN_FILEREF1 - This will contain the actual file object
  • _WEBIN_NAME1 - the value that was specified in the NAME attribute by the frontend

To illustrate with an example - we are uploading two files, F1 and F2. The following JS code will be generated, and inserted at the beginning of the executed program:

const _WEBIN_FILEREF1 = fs.readFileSync('/path/to/file1')
const _WEBIN_FILEREF2 = fs.readFileSync('/path/to/file2')
const _WEBIN_FILENAME1 = 'F1'
const _WEBIN_FILENAME2 = 'F2'
const _WEBIN_NAME1 = 'FormRef1'
const _WEBIN_NAME2 = 'FormRef2'

const _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT = 2

If there are no files uploaded, only the following code will be generated:

const _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT = 0

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The recommended way to send data back is webout(), which mirrors the %ms_webout() macro so that a JS program is laid out the way a SAS one is:

data work.users;
  set work.source;
run;

%ms_webout(OPEN)
%ms_webout(OBJ,users)
%ms_webout(CLOSE)

const users = [{ name: 'ann' }, { name: 'bob' }]

webout('OPEN')
webout('OBJ', 'users', users)
webout('CLOSE')
Action What it does OPEN Truncates the response body, starts one JSON object, and appends content-type: application/json to the response headers. ARR Appends one member to that object: an array of rows, each row a positional array of values. OBJ Appends one member to that object: an array of rows, each row an object keyed by column name. CLOSE Appends the system block below, and closes the JSON object.

The actions are case-insensitive, the member name is the key the frontend reads (res.users), and a table must come between OPEN and CLOSE.

OPEN writes SYSDATE and SYSTIME as the first two members, in the SAS DATE9 and TIME8 forms (02NOV2026, 11:45:32). CLOSE adds the same system fields that %ms_webout(CLOSE) does, carrying the values a JavaScript runtime can answer:

Field Value in a JS program _DEBUG the _debug query parameter _PROGRAM the _program value AUTOEXEC empty - JS has no autoexec MF_GETUSER _SASJS_USERNAME SYSCC 0, or 8 when the program logged an error - see the console mapping below SYSENCODING utf-8 SYSERRORTEXT the last message the program sent to console.error SYSHOSTINFOLONG kernel type, release and architecture of the host (browser user agent in a mock build) SYSHOSTNAME host name (location.hostname in a mock build) SYSPROCESSID, SYSJOBID the interpreter's process id, which in a mock build is the constant 4242 the sandbox supplies - every mock run reports it, including two running at once SYSPROCESSMODE Stored Program SYSPROCESSNAME NodeJS, or Browser in a mock build SYSSCPL the platform, eg linux, or browser in a mock build SYSSITE empty SYSTCPIPHOSTNAME _SASJS_APISERVERURL - the address the program is running on SYSUSERID _SASJS_USERID SYSVLONG the Node version, or browser in a mock build SYSWARNINGTEXT the last message the program sent to console.warn END_DTTM ISO 8601 timestamp of the CLOSE MEMSIZE total memory of the host, in the SIZEKMG form (eg 15.6G); navigator.deviceMemory in a mock build, and empty when the browser does not expose it

Three behaviours worth knowing:

  • CLOSE is the program's job. The server does not close the object for you, exactly as it does not for a SAS program that omits %ms_webout(CLOSE). A program that stops after OPEN returns the truncated body it wrote, which is not valid JSON; the log carries a NOTE naming the missing call. A program that throws after OPEN behaves the way any runtime does on a failed run: the response carries the partial body, then the log separator and the program's log.
  • SYSERRORTEXT and SYSWARNINGTEXT come from the console. SAS fills them from the last error and warning the engine recorded; a JS program has no engine, so the equivalent is the last message it sent to console.error / console.warn. Both calls are still forwarded to the console unchanged, so the session log looks exactly as it did, and SYSCC becomes 8 when an error was logged. Only the last message of each is kept, and only its final 2000 characters.
  • Do not mix webout() with _webout. When webout() has streamed the body, an assignment to _webout is ignored and the log says so.
  • A table before OPEN, a second OPEN, a table after CLOSE, an unknown action, or rows of the wrong shape throws, so the failure lands in the session log rather than in a malformed response. In a mock build the host facts come from the browser and there is no os module; the block asks for one and falls back when it is refused.

docs.title: _SASJS_WEBOUT_HEADERS
docs.text:
This (string) variable points to the location of a text file where header records (such as Content-type: application/zip) can be written. The file starts with a text/html line, and webout('OPEN') appends a content-type: application/json record to it; a program that wants another content type appends its own record afterwards, and the server takes the last record in the file. Sample code:

fs.appendFileSync(_SASJS_WEBOUT_HEADERS, '\ncontent-type: application/zip\n')

Append, never overwrite. fs.writeFileSync truncates the file, so the seeded text/html line and the record webout('OPEN') wrote are both discarded - the content type becomes the one you wrote, and any header the server had already recorded is gone. The leading newline is there because the seeded line carries no trailing one: without it the two records run together on a single line and are read as one.

docs.title: _webout
docs.text: Any content added to this variable is returned to the browser by SASjs Server, and a program that assigns it owns its own content type - the default is text/html. The variable can hold binary or textual content, so this is the route for a response that is not JSON. To send JSON, or to get the system block for free, use webout() above.

docs.title: Python Programs
docs.text:
The use of Python "programs" as your backend is highly beneficial for the following use cases:

  • You would like to test your application in a non SAS environment (such as a CI/CD pipeline or developer machine)
  • You would like to make use of Python packages in your SAS applications
  • You would like to provide backup services in case SAS is unavailable

Any content written to sys.stdout or sys.stderr will be returned in the response "log" (identically to SAS).

docs.title: Input Variables
docs.text:
Any URL parameters (eg &name1=value1&something=else) are attached as Python variables in uppercase, eg as follows:

NAME1='value1'
SOMETHING='else'

A number of "fixed" variables are also added at the start of the program, eg as follows:

_SASJS_TOKENFILE = '/home/sasjssrv/sasjs_root/sessions/20220808081136-29012-1659946296436/reqHeaders.txt';
_SASJS_USERNAME = 'allan';
_SASJS_USERID = '6';
_SASJS_DISPLAYNAME = 'Allan Bowe';
_METAPERSON = _SASJS_DISPLAYNAME;
_METAUSER = _SASJS_USERNAME;
SASJSPROCESSMODE = 'Stored Program';

docs.title: Input Files
docs.text:
Any files attached to a request will be saved in the session folder. The session folder (with the input files) will also be the current folder, eg os.chdir("/path/to/session/folder").

When input files exist, the following variables will also be dynamically added to the Python program:

  • _WEBIN_FILE_COUNT - contains an integer, from 0 to the number of files to being provided. This variable is always created.
  • _WEBIN_FILENAME1 - the value that was specified in the FILENAME attribute by the frontend
  • _WEBIN_NAME1 - the value that was specified in the NAME attribute by the frontend

To illustrate with an example - we are uploading two files to a Python Stored Program, namely f1.txt and f2.xls. The following Python code will be generated, and inserted at the beginning of the executed program:

_WEBIN_FILENAME1 = 'f1.txt'
_WEBIN_FILENAME2 = 'f2.xls'
_WEBIN_NAME1 = 'FormRef1'
_WEBIN_NAME2 = 'FormRef2'

_WEBIN_FILE_COUNT = 2

If there are no files uploaded, only the following code will be generated:

_WEBIN_FILE_COUNT = 0

Note that there are no _WEBIN_FILEREF variables created - in Python it is necessary to know the type of file (eg binary / text) before it can be ingested with the open() function, eg open(_WEBIN_FILENAME1,"rt") or open(_WEBIN_FILENAME2,"rb"). Therefore it is left as an exercise for the developer to ingest as appropriate.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: The following variables are "special":

docs.title: _WEBOUT
docs.text:
This variable points to a text file in the session folder (eg _WEBOUT="/path/to/session/folder/webout.txt"). All content written to _WEBOUT is streamed in the STP API call result.

Example code:

f = open(_WEBOUT, 'w')
f.write('{"hello":"world"}')

docs.title: HEADERSPATH
docs.text:
This variable points to a text file where header records (such as Content-type: application/zip) can be written, eg HEADERSPATH="/path/to/session/folder/headers.txt").

To return data to the client, just write it to the _WEBOUT file. It will then be returned to the browser / client application. Be sure to set the Content-Type in the HEADERSPATH file if it is anything other than JSON.

docs.title: R Programs
docs.text: Stored Programs may also run using the language of R. Any content written to .ROut will be returned in the response "log" (identically to SAS). As R does not support the underscore (_) as the first character in a variable name, the automatic variables are preceded with a period (.) instead.

docs.title: Input Variables
docs.text:
Any URL parameters (eg &name1=value1&something=else) are attached as R variables in uppercase, eg as follows:

NAME1 <- 'value1'
SOMETHING <- 'else'

A number of "fixed" variables are also added at the start of the program, eg as follows:

._SASJS_TOKENFILE <- '/home/sasjssrv/sasjs_root/sessions/20220808081136-29012-1659946296436/reqHeaders.txt';
._SASJS_USERNAME <- 'allan';
._SASJS_USERID <- '6';
._SASJS_DISPLAYNAME <- 'Allan Bowe';
._METAPERSON <- ._SASJS_DISPLAYNAME;
._METAUSER <- ._SASJS_USERNAME;
SASJSPROCESSMODE <- 'Stored Program';
