docs.title: SASjs Studio
docs.text:
Run SAS or JS code in a single interface! Just select your preferred runtime from the dropdown next to the running man.

Running code in SASjs Studio, and switching runtime.

The running man runs the code - the selection when there is one, otherwise the whole buffer - and Ctrl+Enter does the same from the keyboard.

Code is saved in local storage, so you don't lose your work if you close the browser tab.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
The disk icon above the editor saves the file, as does Ctrl+S. When the editor holds changes the drive does not have yet, a blue dot sits on the disk. Saving clears it. While the file matches what the drive holds the disk is greyed out, so a click on it always has something to do.

A JSON file that is minified - one line with no spaces between the tokens - opens indented, so a generated config reads as a document rather than one long line. The editor only re-indents text it can reproduce character for character, so a one-line file with its own spacing, or one that already carries indentation, opens exactly as it is stored. The file on the drive keeps its bytes either way until it is saved.

docs.title: Linting and formatting
docs.text:
SAS code is linted as you edit, about half a second after you stop typing, including changes you have not saved yet. Nothing is executed to do it.

The rules come from a .sasjslint file - the same file sasjs lint reads in a project, and the same set of options. A file in the drive gets the rules from the nearest .sasjslint at or above its folder, so a folder carries its own rules for everything beneath it, and the one at the drive root (/.sasjslint) is the default for everything else, including an untitled buffer. The file is ordinary content on the drive: edit it in the tree and the next lint uses the new rules, with no reload and no restart.

Findings appear above the editor as a count. Expanding it lists each finding, and clicking one moves the editor to that line. Nothing is shown when the buffer is clean.

Formatting applies the same rules. Format Code (Alt+Shift+F, or the format button in the file menu) rewrites the buffer, and Format On Save in Settings > Editor - on by default - formats a SAS file as you save it. Both take the .sasjslint for the file's folder, so a project's indentation, header and naming conventions travel with its content.

docs.title: Clipboard
docs.text: Pasting is a keyboard action - Ctrl+V, or Paste in the editor's own menu. A paste that follows a right or middle click on the code is ignored, so text cannot appear in the program from a mouse gesture. The keyboard is never suppressed: the key press clears that guard before the paste it produces, so Ctrl+V works as usual.

docs.title: SAS specific
docs.text:
The big difference between SASjs Studio and other SAS executors is that every execution is with a CLEAN session.

Every session also runs with the SASjs core macros on the SASAUTOS path, so any of them - mp_abort, mf_getuser, mv_createfolder - can be called from a program without a %include. The server copies the library into the drive's sas/sasautos folder at startup and leaves it alone while the folder exists: delete that folder and restart to pick up a newer release.

Other than that, everything works as you would expect. The log is sent to the log window, and the WEBOUT page contains any content sent to the _webout fileref.

docs.title: JS specific
docs.text: When running JS code, any console.log() statements are sent to the log window, and any content saved in the _webout variable is sent to the webout page.

docs.title: Launch Mode
docs.text:
The launch icon opens the program in a new window (or tab), as a fresh execution of the file on the drive:

/SASjsApi/stp/execute?_program=/Public/subfolder/someprog.sas

Save the file first: the URL names the file on the drive, not the buffer in the editor, so an unsaved change is not part of what runs. The response is the program's own output, which makes the URL usable from a bookmark, a scheduler or another application.

docs.title: Testing VA embedding
docs.text:
An application embedded in a SAS Visual Analytics report as a data-driven content (DDC) object is not loaded like a page, and the difference is more than cosmetics. Two things change, and both change what the application sees:

  • The frame carries VA's sandbox attribute set, so anything the app claims from the browser (popups, downloads, same-origin access, storage) is decided against that policy.
  • VA posts its data message to the object as the document appears, which is before the application has bootstrapped. An app that only registers its message listener once it is running misses that first message entirely.

The second point is the one that produces defects nobody can reproduce outside a report. On a report refresh VA replays the report's stored parameters in that first message, so the app has to act on it without having fetched any metadata; a selection the user makes later produces a second message while the app is running, and takes a different path through the same code. A page that works when a message is posted into it can still fail on refresh.

/ddc-host supplies the hosting side of that contract: the sandbox attribute set, and a message delivered on a timing of your choosing.

docs.title: Enable it
docs.text:
The page is off by default. Set DDC_HOST_ENABLED on a development server:

DDC_HOST_ENABLED=YES

Both the page and its script answer 404 while the setting is off. It frames whatever URL it is given, which is useful in development and is why it does not belong on a server a browser user can reach.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
GET /ddc-host takes its configuration from the query string, so a whole scenario is one URL:

Parameter Meaning url Application URL to embed. The page mounts it as soon as the page loads. message JSON posted into the frame. Empty or absent posts nothing. timing load, early or both. Default load. interval Milliseconds between posts in the early replay. Default 50. sandbox Overrides the sandbox attribute set. Defaults to VA's: allow-forms allow-presentation allow-same-origin allow-scripts allow-downloads allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox. height Iframe height in pixels. Default 600. title Heading and page title.

The script is a separate file at /ddc-host.js, behind the same setting, because the server's default policy allows scripts from its own origin only: an inline script on the page is refused by the browser, and the failure looks like an app that does not work rather than a blocked page.

docs.title: Timings
docs.text:
The timing is what makes the difference between the two paths above.

timing Delivery Reproduces load One post when the frame fires its load event. A user interaction: the app is running, has its data, and receives a message. early Posted repeatedly from the moment the frame is created, until the app captures one, the frame loads, or 30 seconds pass. A report refresh: the message lands while the document is still parsing, so the app has to answer it without metadata. both The early replay, then one more post on load. The two messages a refresh can produce in sequence.

early stops on evidence rather than on a timer where it can: a same-origin application that captures the message at parse time publishes what it captured, and the page reads that value to decide it has landed. A cross-origin application cannot be read, so the replay simply runs until the frame loads, which covers the same window.

Because the replay posts the same message more than once, an application under test has to treat a repeated identical message as one action. An app that applies every message it receives will apply the same filter several times.

docs.title: Worked example: Data Controller
docs.text:
Data Controller is the reference implementation - its ?embed=va mode is documented in the Data Controller docs - and its Cypress suite drives this page.

Build the app, deploy it with its services to a local server, then frame it on a filtered route:

# from the application repo, with its mock target pointing at this server
npm run build
cd sas/mocks/sasjs
sasjs cbd -t server-ci          # streams the build to /app/<service name>
sasjs request services/admin/makedata -t server-ci -d deploy/makedata.json

A deploy replaces the destination folder, so seed any data the deploy does not carry after every deploy, not once at the start.

The message is the VA one, with parameters carrying the filter the report holds:

{
  "version": "1",
  "resultName": "dd1",
  "rowCount": 0,
  "availableRowCount": 0,
  "data": [],
  "columns": [],
  "parameters": [
    { "name": "pr1", "label": "SOME_DATE", "dataType": "string", "value": "August 02, 1971" }
  ]
}

Encode that as the message parameter, and the app URL as url:

http://localhost:5000/ddc-host?url=<encoded app url>&message=<encoded json>&timing=early

The app URL points at the route the report object opens, including whatever query string the app needs to recognise the embed, for example http://localhost:5000/app/clickme/#/editor/DC_JSLIB.MPE_X_TEST?embed=va.

docs.title: Reading the result
docs.text:
Three places to look, in increasing order of trustworthiness:

  1. The page's own log, at the bottom of /ddc-host. It records the mount, the sandbox set, each capture attempt, when the frame loaded, and every message that arrives from the frame. This is the only signal available for a cross-origin application.
  2. The frame's state, for a same-origin application: the page reads the app's earliest captured message to stop the replay, so document.getElementById('frame').contentWindow exposes it, together with the frame's current route.
  3. What the application did with the message. This is the assertion worth keeping: the harness only shows that a message arrived, while the app's own effect - a stored filter, a changed route, a service call - is what a user would see. In Data Controller's case the mock public/validatefilter stores the clause it is sent, so the clause can be read back from the drive afterwards.

A capture in the page's log before the frame's load line is what distinguishes the early path from the loaded one. That ordering, not the app's own output, is the fact that makes the case meaningful: the same value can be formatted correctly on both paths, so an assertion on the outcome alone cannot tell you which path produced it.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a VA emulator. There is no report, no data and no rendering: the page is the host side of the contract only, and it sends what you give it.
  • Not a test runner. It gives a browser a scenario; the assertions belong to the app's own suite.
  • Not a proxy for the app's back-channel. Messages the app posts to window.parent appear in the page log, which is enough to see that they happened and what they carried, but the page does not act on them.
